questions.question_text: Which unit is most suitable for a cough-medicine dose?

options.why: Uses a large-capacity unit for a dose of only a few spoonfuls.
Chooses a length unit instead of a capacity unit.
Chooses a mass unit instead of a capacity unit.

questions.solution_text: A medicine dose is a small liquid amount, so millilitres are suitable.

questions.question_text: Which unit is most suitable for the capacity of a wheelbarrow tub?

options.why: Uses a tiny-capacity unit for a container that holds many litres.
Chooses a length unit instead of a capacity unit.
Chooses a mass unit instead of a capacity unit.

questions.solution_text: A wheelbarrow tub holds a large amount, so litres are suitable.

questions.question_text: Which is a sensible capacity for an eye-drop bottle?

options.why: Keeps the number but uses a unit far too large for a small bottle.
Uses both an oversized number and an oversized unit.
Uses an amount smaller than a single useful dose for the whole bottle.

questions.solution_text: A small eye-drop bottle can sensibly hold about $15$ mL.

questions.question_text: Which is a sensible capacity for a kitchen sink?

options.why: Keeps the number but uses an amount smaller than a small cup.
Uses a drop-sized amount for a large basin.
Uses a tank-sized amount for a kitchen sink.

questions.solution_text: A sink can hold tens of litres, so $25$ L is sensible.

questions.question_text: A hand-sanitiser bottle is marked $300$ L. What is the most likely correction?

options.why: Divides the number by ten but leaves the unit as litres, which is still far too large for a bottle held in one hand.
Multiplies by ten instead of changing the unit, making an already impossible capacity ten times worse.
Rewrites $300$ L as $0.3$ kL and then copies the mL label onto that number, giving less than one drop.

questions.solution_text: A hand-held bottle commonly holds hundreds of millilitres, not litres.

questions.question_text: Which pair uses the more suitable units?

options.why: Reverses the small- and large-capacity units.
Uses millilitres for both and makes the pool unit impractical.
Uses litres for both and makes the teaspoon unit impractical.

questions.solution_text: A teaspoon holds a small amount in mL, while a pool holds a large amount in L.
